extracted.intended_audience: chemists and students performing experimental (pneumatic) analysis of gases/air
extracted.subtask_description: Experimental methods and interpretive principles for decomposing, recomposing, and quantifying the constituent gases of atmospheric air using mercury calcination, metal combustion, and related pneumatic apparatus; includes apparatus design, measurement corrections, and interpretive cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise nomenclature for heat-related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use distinct, strictly defined terms for heat concepts: 'calorique libre', 'calorique combiné', 'calorique spécifique', 'capacité pour contenir le calorique', 'chaleur latente', 'chaleur sensible' — these are not synonymous and must be distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defines each term (e.g. calorique libre = not engaged in combination; calorique combiné = chained in bodies by affinity), and emphasizes fixing their strict meanings before experimental discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of thermometer readings
rubrics_metrics.description: A thermometer indicates displacement of caloric among bodies, not the total quantity of caloric released or absorbed by the whole system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thermometric change announces only the portion of caloric received by that instrument in relation to its mass and heat capacity; to measure total caloric released/absorbed use calorimetric methods (e.g. ice-sphere method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calorimetric measurement by ice-sphere (de la Place method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the total quantity of caloric liberated by a body, place the body at the center of a hollow sphere of ice and measure the amount of ice melted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mass of melted ice is an exact expression of the caloric given off. The apparatus built on this idea can determine heat required for state changes and relative caloric quantities of gases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider atmospheric pressure limits on vaporization
rubrics_metrics.description: When reasoning about atmosphere composition under temperature changes, account for the counteracting effect of increasing atmospheric weight (pressure) that limits further vaporization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with strong heating, added vapor increases atmospheric pressure which in turn suppresses further vaporization; thus atmospheric composition reaches a bound rather than unlimited vaporization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-method approach to chemical analysis (composition and decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the nature of a substance by both composition (recombining constituents) and decomposition (separating constituents); satisfaction requires concordant evidence from both methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to air: decompose air into components (e.g. by mercury calcination or metal combustion) and recombine them to verify you recover the original properties of atmospheric air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and sealing of pneumatic apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an airtight setup: a matras/flask with long neck placed in a furnace and connected to a bell jar in a mercury bath; maintain careful sealing and mark mercury heights to measure gas volume changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curved neck to fit furnace, careful suction via siphon under bell jar to raise mercury and mark initial levels; monitor barometer/thermometer throughout. Multiple repetitions may be necessary to retain reaction products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of temperature/time for mercury calcination
rubrics_metrics.description: Calcination of mercury is carried out by heating in a closed vessel for extended periods (e.g. nearly to boiling for days) to produce red oxide and effect decomposition of air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: maintain heat almost continuously for twelve days until calcination progress ceases. Observe formation of red particles and record volume changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass–volume balance to infer gas composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh solid/liquid products (e.g. red mercury oxide) and correlate the loss or gain of mass with measured changes in gas volume to deduce amounts and densities of gas components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 45 grains of red matter yielded 41.5 grains of condensed mercury and 7–8 cubic inches of an elastic fluid; use these mass and volume measurements to characterize the separated gas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and recombination test for gas components
rubrics_metrics.description: Show air consists of two elastic fluids (respirable and non-respirable) by separating them and recombining in measured proportions to reproduce atmospheric air properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After separating by calcination, recombine the residual 'mofète' (non-respirable) and the respirable portion in the proper volume ratio and verify combustion and animal respiration are restored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reactive metals (iron) for rapid decomposition of air
rubrics_metrics.description: Burning iron in pure respirable air rapidly consumes the respirable component, producing a measurable decrease in gas volume and an increase in metal weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange iron spirals and ignition under a bell jar of pure respirable air; measure initial and final gas volumes (via mercury levels) and weigh iron residues to compute absorbed gas mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize gas volumes to reference temperature and pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Always correct measured gas volumes to a common standard (example: 10 degrees temperature and 28 inches mercury) before comparing or calculating quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists on reducing volumes at start and end of experiments to these conditions and promises details on these corrections elsewhere in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus safety and limits on quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the quantity of reactive metal burned and ensure strong glassware to avoid violent failures (glass breakage due to abrupt pressure/temperature changes and mercury column movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: under an 8-pint bell jar do not burn more than about 1.5 gros (approx.) of iron; otherwise the capsule may rise, crack the bell, and cause dangerous mercury surges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-reaction characterization of residual gas
rubrics_metrics.description: After combustion and cooling, remove residues and submit the remaining gas to chemical tests (potash, sulfide of potash, etc.) and to water displacement to characterize its properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce reagents under the same bell jar, then displace mercury with water to transfer gas to pneumatic apparatus for larger-scale testing; select reagents appropriate to suspected gas identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reagent and sample impurities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that metals (e.g. iron, steel) and sampled respirable air commonly contain impurities (carbon, traces of non-respirable gas) which affect results and must be considered in interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When iron contains carbon, the residual gas or product composition can be affected; the respirable portion is rarely perfectly pure. Such impurities usually don't invalidate conclusions but must be tracked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify composition by volume (expected proportions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect the atmospheric composition (in the climates examined) to be approximately 27 parts respirable air to 73 parts non-respirable (by volume).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes uncertainties and proposes to discuss causes of inexactness later; this is an empirical approximate ratio inferred from multiple experimental routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for dissolved water in gas analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Air and other elastic fluids dissolve water; when measuring or comparing gaseous volumes, account for water content (e.g. Saussure's estimate of 12 grains of water per cubic foot of air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humidity can produce special phenomena and has led to experimental errors; proper experimental technique must control or correct for dissolved water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt simple, fixed names after identification
rubrics_metrics.description: After analyzing and identifying constituents, replace provisional periphrases ('partie respirable', 'partie non respirable') with fixed simple nomenclature for clarity in further discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author transitions from descriptive phrases to concise terms once chemical distinctions are established, improving communication and precision in subsequent chapters.
